name: On the Value of Sente (Nordic Go Dojo)
one_line: Explains sente (initiative-forcing move) vs gote, and models the value of sente as the point-gap between alternating descending move values (e.g. 4,3,2,1 -> sente worth 2 points net).
take_what: A concrete forcing-move economy: rank available plays by 'threat value', and whoever holds initiative always grabs the current-highest-value play while the responder is stuck answering. Give Limen tiles an explicit 'forcing' flag (like siege/menace) that obligates a same-turn-or-next-turn response, and track who is spending turns responding vs. who is choosing freely - surface this as a visible 'initiative' indicator.

name: Connection Games III: Havannah and Starweb (Dr Eric Silverman)
one_line: Breaks down Havannah's three simultaneous win conditions (ring, fork, bridge) and Starweb's triangular-number scoring that rewards a 'minority strategy' of raiding instead of hoarding corners.
take_what: Havannah forces players to threaten and defend three different win shapes at once, which is what keeps placement tense across the whole board instead of players building safely in a corner. Concretely: Starweb's score formula rewards CONNECTED clusters superlinearly (n+(n-1)+...+1), which makes turtling in one corner strictly worse than contesting multiple fronts - directly answers Limen's 'players build up in their own corners' problem.

name: Moyo (Go term) - GoMagic + AllAboutGo
one_line: Moyo is a loose framework of stones that projects influence over open space but is not secured territory; conventionally valued at ~50% of its eventual territorial worth until enclosed, and is always subject to invasion/reduction.
take_what: A discounted-potential-territory rule: unclaimed hexes adjacent to a player's influence web count at half value toward a running score/threat meter, but ONLY until an opponent tile physically touches that space (invasion), at which point the discount is voided. This gives corner-building players a soft incentive to actually contest rather than just stack influence numbers passively - turns the existing influence math into a felt spatial claim.

name: Yavalath rules and forced-move strategy
one_line: Cameron Browne's machine-evolved connection game: make 4-in-a-row to win, but making 3-in-a-row (without also making 4) is an instant loss - so the real skill is forcing the OPPONENT into an unavoidable 3-in-a-row.
take_what: A self-endangering aggression rule: overextending a formation can trigger your own loss condition, so players must attack via forced moves rather than brute stacking. Applied to Limen: a tile-placement pattern that creates 3+ of your own tiles in an unbroken adjacent line (or ring) without a capital/anchor tile could trigger a small self-penalty (influence drain), forcing players to break their own turtle shapes and reach across the board instead of piling tiles safely.
constraint: none - open rules, would need reskinning to hex-influence math

name: Developing Tak (Crab Fragment Labs, James Ernest)
one_line: Designer postmortem on Tak: switching the win condition from area-scoring to road-building made the game 'faster, with earlier excitement,' and the capstone (flattens enemy walls, can't be stacked on) was added specifically to break monotony between the two existing piece types.
take_what: Two transferable numbers: (1) making the PRIMARY win condition reachable early/fast (a 'road' can complete well before the board fills) rather than an end-game score tally - directly attacks Limen's slow-start problem; (2) a single limited 'wildcard' piece (1 capstone/player) that can override normal stacking rules (flatten a wall) as the one high-impact tempo tool, which is a template for a rare high-influence 'siege-breaker' tile.
constraint: Tak is commercial IP (Cheapass Games) - reference the design lesson, don't clone the piece names/art

name: Tak rules - stack movement and carry limits
one_line: In Tak, a stack's top piece controls ownership; a move can pick up and 'carry' up to (board-size) stones from the top of a stack and drop them one-per-hex along a straight line, redistributing control as it goes.
take_what: A carry-and-drop movement mechanic for stacks: instead of static towers, let a max-3 tower in Limen 'unstack' by moving its top N tiles in a line to adjacent hexes, redistributing influence bonuses as it goes. This turns tower-building from a purely defensive stat-stack into an offensive maneuver with real board-shape consequences - directly targets Limen's 'placement lacks strategic feeling' problem by giving stacks a use beyond sitting still.
constraint: Tak's exact carry/drop rule is IP of Cheapass Games/James Ernest - implement the underlying idea (top-controls-ownership, redistribute-on-move) with different exact numbers

name: Ladder (Go) - Wikipedia
one_line: A ladder is a forced zigzag capture sequence: each atari (capture threat) forces exactly one legal response, so the whole sequence is calculable from the first move, and whether a 'ladder breaker' stone exists elsewhere on the board changes the correct move dozens of tiles away.
take_what: The 'ladder breaker' concept: a single stone placed far from the current fight can retroactively make a forced sequence favorable or unfavorable, meaning good players read board-wide interactions before starting a local fight. For Limen, this suggests exposing an 'if I place here, does it set up an inevitable capture chain elsewhere' preview/highlight - not a rules change but a UI/legibility feature that makes the existing influence math feel spatial and forward-looking rather than purely local arithmetic.

name: Atari (Go term) - GoMagic
one_line: Atari is the state of a stone/group with exactly one liberty left - a direct, unmissable capture threat that forces an immediate opposing response or loss of the group.
take_what: A binary, loudly-telegraphed 'one step from death' state (not a hidden math threshold). Limen's capture rule (effective influence <=0) is currently a quiet number comparison; borrowing atari's UX - a hard visual/audio state change the instant a tile crosses '1 point from capturable' - would make the existing math read as a threat rather than a spreadsheet check, addressing the 'placement lacks strategic feeling' problem without touching the underlying formula.

name: Connection Game overview - Wikipedia
one_line: Surveys the connection-game genre (Hex, Havannah, TwixT, Y, Slither) and the shared design principle that connection games avoid draws by construction and reward contesting shared, contested cells rather than building in safe isolated regions.
take_what: The genre-level design axiom that a connection game's win condition should make EVERY empty cell matter to both players simultaneously (no cell is 'purely mine' until claimed) - the opposite of Limen's current corner-building pattern where early tiles are placed with no opposing stake in them. Concretely: a scarce-resource overlay (e.g. only N total 'capital-adjacent' or rift-adjacent hexes exist) that both players are pulled toward from turn 1 would force early contact.

name: Strategies I've picked up from a few games of Tak (community gist)
one_line: Player-written strategy notes: walls (standing stones) are cheap tempo plays that block a road without committing a flat stone, and skilled play centers on threatening two roads at once so the opponent can only block one.
take_what: The 'double threat' pattern from a player's own words: build toward two simultaneous winning lines so a single-tile response can't cover both. Limen's capture-from-anywhere rule already supports non-adjacent threats; explicitly designing a small set of 'dual-threat' rite/keyword combos (e.g. a rite that threatens both a capital rush and a mass-capture) would let players create Tak-style forks instead of single-line pushes.
